_note: The substrate profile registry. One rule split: the founding Earth substrate is admitted by recomputability from free public archives and serves as the standing drift anchor; every device-borne substrate is admitted only with its complete, unaltered OS execution trace (emem.os_trace.v1, verified by emem-trace). Grain is the measurement grain in meters; microscope profiles reach into microns. Candidate status means the profile is pinned for device makers to build against, not that ingest is open. Every profile also declares its address_space: geo.cell64 for everything that observes a place, entity.cid for subjects that have no latitude. A profile may only be `active` on an address space this build can key a fact by, which today is geo.cell64 alone, so the entity.cid profiles are pinned as candidates for builders rather than advertised as ingest.

substrates.title: Earth observation from open satellite archives
substrates._note: The founding substrate and the drift anchor. Its four evidence layers are what a reader can cross-score: trace is the transparency log and receipt chain, signal is the raw band and Fourier encodings, inference is the foundation-model embeddings with their served_via record, weather is the forcing context. Admission needs no OS trace because every cited source is a public archive a third party can re-fetch. The archives publish no OS traces; what they do publish is declared processing lineage (the SAFE manifest, the STAC processing properties, and the Copernicus Data Space traceability register of per-product BLAKE3 checksums), listed under declared_lineage.

substrates.title: Operator-contributed satellites, downlink under the operator's key
substrates._note: The profile for a satellite manufacturer or operator contributing its own constellation's data, distinct from earth.satellite.v0: that profile is the open public archive, admitted by recomputability; this one is a device substrate like any other, admitted only with the platform's OS execution trace. The trace comes from the flight or payload computer (RTOS encodings like zephyr.ctf.v1, or the ground-segment ingest host as a first step), with energy and thermal required because power and thermal telemetry are the spacecraft tracks hardest to fabricate consistently. Operator writes are drift-scored against the open archive where bands overlap, which is exactly the cross-check a proprietary constellation cannot self-provide.

substrates.title: An orbital payload attesting itself with the counters a hardened Linux container can read
substrates._note: Same substrate as orbital.satellite.v1, lower evidence bar, and the two differences are the whole point. Named so that it does NOT nest inside orbital.satellite.v1's string: this was orbital.satellite.counters.v1, the only id in this registry that contained another, and a consumer skimming a record's profile field - or matching on a prefix - could read it as the stronger profile. A _note is read by someone who already stopped to look; the id is read by everyone else. The same reasoning that keeps a counter segment labelled linux.procfs.v1 rather than linux.ftrace.v1 applies to the profile that requires it. That profile requires syscall, sensor_bus, signal, energy and thermal, and demands provenance_class attested_execution. A payload computer running a hardened container - no tracefs, no CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, no ROS2, no hwmon paths - can satisfy none of it, because sensor_bus and signal have no registered encoding but ros2.bag.v2. An operator in that position was left choosing between a profile whose name is true and whose traces are never cited, and host.counters.v1, whose traces cite but whose name says the spacecraft is a generic host. The profile is signed into every record and cannot be corrected afterwards, so that is not a choice anyone should have to make. This profile is the honest third answer: every substrate field is copied from orbital.satellite.v1 unchanged - contributor_class satellite, address_space geo.cell64, grain, tempo - so a record under it says orbital node just as truly, without borrowing the stronger profile's identifier to do it. WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM: provenance_class is direct_sensor, NOT attested_execution. The four required layers come from /proc/schedstat, /proc/meminfo, /proc/diskstats and /proc/net/dev, carried as linux.procfs.v1 segments, which are counters read at two instants rather than an ordered log of what ran. A record under this profile binds its payload digests to a device key, a clock and a machine that was demonstrably doing something. It does not attest which code produced them. A consumer that needs execution evidence must require a profile naming syscall, and must not treat this as orbital.satellite.v1 with a longer name.

substrates.title: Telescopes observing from a fixed site cell
substrates._note: Native resolution is angular; the grain range states the spatial grain at typical subject distances and is indicative only. The site cell is the anchor address; the observation carries its own pointing metadata.

substrates.title: Laboratory and field microscopes
substrates._note: Grain runs from 100 nanometers to 100 microns. The lab's cell is the anchor address; sample identity is an emem:entity: the observation cites.

substrates.title: Fixed surveillance and monitoring cameras
substrates._note: The simplest device case: one location, one key, a stream of observations. Privacy classes apply before anything derived from imagery of people is written.

substrates.title: Phones and wearables
substrates._note: A moving attester with on-device models in the path, so the inference layer is required: which weights ran over which input is part of the evidence.

substrates.title: Survey drones
substrates._note: A flight is a moving attester writing along a path; each observation lands at the cell it measured, inside the flight's trace window.

substrates.title: Robot fleets
substrates._note: The lighthouse profile. Upgrades the fleet-memory example from bare HTTP writes to trace-bound writes: two vendors' robots share one map, and each write carries the execution evidence the other vendor can verify without a shared backend.

substrates.title: Meters, turbines, plant-floor machines
substrates._note: Location-pinned observations whose trace shows exactly which process produced the value, down to energy and thermal tracks.

substrates.title: Fixed gauges and single-purpose sensors
substrates._note: The minimum trace floor: even a river gauge on a microcontroller OS presents its syscall and sensor-bus layers. A device that cannot trace cannot write.

substrates.title: Targets observed off Earth, where the subject has no latitude
substrates._note: A telescope SITE has a cell; the thing it looks at does not. observatory.telescope.v1 addresses the site and is geo.cell64. This profile addresses the TARGET, and is the clearest case for entity.cid: there is no latitude of a body that is not on this planet. Subjects are anchored, not located: `sky:<nside>.<pix>` for a pointing and `orb:s<shell>.i<inc>.o<raan>.p<slot>` for an object, both QUANTISED on purpose so two observers who disagree slightly still resolve to one subject rather than two adjacent ones. The bands and that anchor design come from dpwotikn's fourteen-message handoff (`pqbrf5vlpjxan44peptluk4hnq`), a working neuromorphic RSO detector on a 0.8 m station. Read their failures before building on it: five of ten public recordings fail, the bright branch fires 0.775 false detections per window on background-only sky, p95 exceeds a 40 ms budget on 11.8 percent of 1280x720 windows, and their headline polarity matched filter does not transfer, the discriminating contrast having the opposite sign on six of ten recordings. What DID hold is the part that matters to a memory protocol: signed provenance cost 0.167 percent of the frame budget entirely off the hot path, and 399 of 399 facts verified offline. Absence is first-class here rather than exceptional: for a geostationary search, `observed and nothing there` is the normal result, not an error.

substrates.title: Source code at a commit
substrates._note: Admitted by recomputability for the same reason the Earth archives are, and the fit is closer than it looks: git is already a content-addressed store, so a third party re-fetching a commit gets byte-identical trees. The subject is a file or symbol at a commit, which is an identity and not a place. The value emem adds over git is the half git does not do: a signed reading ABOUT the code at that address, cross-attester contradiction when two analysers disagree, and a bi-temporal answer to what we believed about this function in May.

substrates.title: A table or column at a schema version
substrates._note: The subject is a table or column at a schema version, and the readings are the statistics people already compute and then cannot defend: a null rate, a cardinality, a freshness lag. Those numbers travel between teams as screenshots today. Recomputability holds only against an immutable snapshot; a live table is not re-fetchable, and a profile that pretended otherwise would be admitting values nobody can check.

substrates.title: A model at a checkpoint, and what was measured of it
substrates._note: Every encoder record already pins its checkpoint, so this generalises a thing the Earth substrate does rather than inventing one: a model swap must never pose as change in the world. Here the model IS the subject. An eval score is the reading, and it is worth addressing for the same reason a band value is: two labs quoting one benchmark are usually quoting two, and contradiction scoring at a shared address is what shows that rather than arguing about it.

substrates.title: A span in an execution trace, as the subject rather than the evidence
substrates._note: emem already verifies OS execution traces, but only as EVIDENCE that a device's reading of the world is admissible. This profile makes the trace the subject: the reading is about the run itself, its latency, its allocation, its syscall shape. Same verifier, same required layers, inverted role. It stays os_trace_required because a run cannot be re-fetched the way an archive can; the trace is the only thing that makes it checkable at all.

substrates.title: A general-purpose host attesting itself with the counters Linux gives anyone
substrates._note: The profile a Linux host can actually satisfy without privilege. Every other os_trace profile requires sensor_bus, signal or inference, whose only registered encodings are ros2.bag.v2, linux.ebpf.raw and nvidia.nsys.v1; a host without that stack can satisfy none of them, and exec.trace.v1 needs syscall, which needs a tracefs mount and the capability to read it. A hosted payload on a read-only rootfs with neither could therefore produce a signed, chained, payload-binding trace that NO profile would admit, which was reported from a real deployment. The four layers here come from /proc/schedstat, /proc/meminfo, /proc/diskstats and /proc/net/dev: present on every Linux, readable by any uid, no mount and no capability. WHAT THIS IS NOT: those segments carry encoding linux.procfs.v1, which is a counter read at two instants, not linux.ftrace.v1, which is an ordered log of what happened. A counter delta is real evidence that a machine was doing something during a window, and it binds the payload digests emitted in that window to a device key and a clock. It is not evidence of WHICH code ran, and a consumer that needs that must require a profile that names syscall. Candidate rather than active: it is here so a device with no kernel tracing has something true to say, not because counter-level evidence should quietly become the norm.
